references.text: Amos warns those who live in security and abundance in Zion, a parallel to Jesus' woe to the rich who have already received their comfort.
Isaiah pronounces woe on those who add house to house and field to field – a prophetic warning against wealth and greed that mirrors Jesus' words against the rich.
The one who trusts in their riches will fall – a wisdom literature parallel to the warning that the rich have already received their comfort.

In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Abraham says: 'Remember that you received your good things during your lifetime.' This is a direct parallel to the statement that the rich have already received their comfort (παράκλησιν).
The parable of the rich farmer who stored up wealth for himself but was not rich toward God illustrates the danger of placing one's trust in earthly prosperity.
James pronounces woe on the rich and warns that their wealth has rotted – a New Testament parallel to Jesus' woe to the rich in the Beatitudes.
Paul warns that those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a trap, for the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil – an apostolic exhortation that aligns with Jesus' warning.
The blessing on the poor forms a contrast to the woe against the rich: the poor will inherit God's kingdom, while the rich have already received their comfort.

Jesus says that the hypocrites who perform good deeds to be seen by others have already received their reward (ἀπέχουσιν τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν) – the same verb ἀπέχω is used regarding the rich who have received their comfort.
Babylon the Great, who lived in luxury and abundance and said she would never see sorrow, receives her judgment – an eschatological picture of the false security of wealth.
